subject: health
unitTitle: Mental and Emotional Health: Stress, Coping, and Help-Seeking
title: Launch and diagnostic: the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood
focus: the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood
essentialQuestion: How do I manage stress in a way that still works on a bad week, and how do I ask for help early?
materials: a guardian-approved list of local and national help resources
keyPoints: The stress response can alter attention, sleep, mood, muscle tension, and heart rate; short activation can be useful, while sustained disruption is a reason to add recovery and support.
Match the response to the level of need: use a practical coping step for ordinary strain, add trusted support when functioning is disrupted, and use urgent help for immediate danger.

For the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Build a two-tier support plan: strategies the learner can run alone, and the named point at which they contact a trusted adult or professional. The plan may be written entirely with general categories rather than personal detail.
studentTask: Complete a fictional support-plan card for the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood: identify one observable signal, choose one immediate coping or communication step, name a routine support route and an urgent route, and explain why the plan does not make a peer responsible for care.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: Coping strategies may be movement-based, still, sensory, verbal, written, or silent; every learner selects strategies their body and setting actually allow. Responses may be selected from options rather than composed.
extensionChallenge: Apply the stress response and what it does to attention, sleep, and mood under a new constraint, compare two approaches, or explain the idea to someone else with an original fictional example, without completing another learner's graded work.
accessibilitySupports: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
